utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that the parties would like to raise further disclosure issues. An opportunity will be given for that later today. The witness is -- or is is there any urgency in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think we've been made aware of what the issues are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Then perhaps I'm misinformed. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We'd like -- in fact Mr. Russo is here only for the first session and unfortunately not after 6.00. We'd like to raise to an issue which was triggered yesterday by your acceptance of the offer by Mr. Theunens to deliver his expert report which triggered e-mail responses from the Defence this morning. I would just like to clarify a couple of issues in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Theunens is here now. I don't suggest that if Mr. Russo is available during the first session that -- how much time would you need? Three minutes or five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like not to answer the question. But we can do it at the beginning of the second session if that suits you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then at least we -- first of all, I don't know how appropriate that will be for Mr. Theunens to be the witness of -- of what we discuss about disclosure issues apparently triggered by your kind gesture yesterday, Mr. Theunens, to provide earlier versions. We will do it, then, at the beginning of the second session. But this is not a way to -- the reason why I'm usually scheduling procedural matters at the end is because then you are limited in time. The same limits apply if you will raise the issue in the beginning of the second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Waespi, could you give us any indication as how long you would deal with the -- with the issue you started with as the Chamber requested you to do. That is, the issue of expertise, scope of expertise, and the other matter was the methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it is probably another half an hour, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another half an hour. We would then give an opportunity to Defence to deal with that before we go to the substance of the report. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before we go into the detail of your methodology, I would like to kind of finish your CV, and we did not really look at your CV and did not tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter 6100 could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You're familiar with your CV, obviously. Is there anything you would like to add or clarify to the CV that you see displayed on the screen very soon?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the CV that was attached to the report when it was filed in December 2007. Just a small update, as I mentioned yesterday, in the meanwhile I testified in the trial of Vojislav Seselj; that happened in February 2007. And I testified on the basis of an expert report titled, Role of SRS/SJP volunteers in the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. And also as we mentioned yesterday, on the 12th of September -- excuse me, on the 13th of September, I spoke at a conference in Oslo on the use -- on the role of military expertise in laying criminal charges. That conference was also attended by Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could tender this piece of evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. No objections, I see. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit number P1112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1112 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Last point on the time you were part of the Belgian Ministry of Defence. Did you also acquire knowledge about the special police that was deployed in -- in Croatia while you were part of the Belgian MOD?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. We considered the activities, and I use that term in a very general manner, of the special police together with the activities of the Guards Brigades and also a unit known as the 1st Guards or the Presidential Guard as key indicators for possible contentions of the Croatian armed forces in relation to the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let's move to the methodology in more detail. Yesterday, you described the sources you relied upon to which you had access to. Now, can you tell us, and I know you described it in your previous testimonies as an expert in detail, but please again walk us through the process, how you transformed these sources into your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the methodology I applied is commonly known as the intelligence cycle. The intelligence cycle covers four phases. The first one, direction; then there is collection; third one is processing; and the last one is dissemination. These are what is called discrete phases, i.e., they happen simultaneously and they interact with each other. And if you want, I can go into more details of these phases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please. And please address when you start addressing direction and then tell us when you talk about collection and processing and lastly, dissemination, so we see the steps under each of those four headings. Let's start about direction, concretely in this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this case, direction consisted of the lists I received and which were discussed yesterday, i.e., the ten-point and subsequently the 17-point -- 17-item list, whereby in response I proposed a draft outline or table of contents. Once this draft outline was approved by Mr. Tieger, I used that outline in order to focus my further efforts and that is meant by direction. In the collection phase, as the word says it, I started to collect information. We mentioned yesterday, for example, what kind of documents I looked at, whereby this collection was driven by obviously the direction, i.e., the specific nature of information I required based on the draft outline. In the processing phase, the information is transformed into intelligence. What is meant by that in the processing phase, five steps will be carried out. First of all, the information that has been collected will be collated, which means it will be organised by team or by topic, electronically in hard copy and so on. Secondly, which is -- the second step, which is a very important step in this context, is the evaluation step. During the evaluation step of the processing phase, the information will be appraised from two aspects. First of all, the reliability of the source; and secondly, the credibility of the information. A reliable source can provide information of low credibility and vice versa. Again, if you wish more details I can explain in detail what is meant. Basically, reliability means -- reliability goes to aspects like what is the relation between the source and the information, what is the reputation of the source, does the source have any particular interest in relation to the information, and so on. Credibility of the information deals with, well, has the information been corroborated by other sources, is the information coherent with what we know already. Because we never start from zero. Anyway, in the next step of the processing phase, the information will be analysed which means that we will review the newly collected information in order to identify relevant facts for subsequent interpretation. According to doctrine analysis is followed by integration, which means that -- actually, integration is difficult to disassociate from analysis because it happens more or less mentally at the same time. The information will be organised in patterns, but it is a mental process. And after analysis and integration, we will interpret the information, in order to determine what the significance is of the information compared to what we know already. So that covers the processing phase. The last phase, the dissemination phase, basically is the report, i.e., the analysed information which has become intelligence, because of the mental processes I just described, will be presented in a manner that is, according to doctrine, timely and appropriate. To conclude this intelligence cycle is something I was first -- first learned about in Military Academy. It's applied in most armed forces or in most intelligence services, even though I realize, that for example, in United States there is a slightly different identification of the different steps, and also criminal analysts, there is a slightly different denomination of the different steps and phases, but it -- at the end it all comes to the same process, which, as I mentioned, especially where processing is concerned, is a mental process, which is obviously determined by the training, education, and experience of the analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Now you mentioned that you applied the methodology of an intelligence analyst. From your experience as an expert in other cases, in preparing drafts, in testifying, do you see any differences in the analysis carried out by an analyst and an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, traditionally, an intelligence analyst will predict events, i.e., he or she looks at certain events that have happened and will try to make a prediction in order to determine what can happen in the future. Here the role is almost the opposite. Here the analysis or the intelligence cycle is applied in order to explain certain events or to describe them. So in summary, I would say that traditional intelligence analysis is about predicting, whereas here my role, as well as of colleague analysts, criminal analysts or military analyst in the OTP, is about describing or explaining. But in my view, the same mental processes apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me follow up with a couple of concrete situations or examples. How did you determine the relevancy of the documents to be included into the report and what criteria did you use to include them or not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I compared with the activities I described yesterday, i.e., the professional activities I carried out before joining the ICTY. I saw myself, especially in this case, in what I would describe as a very privileged situation because there's such a huge amount of what I would call firsthand source material available. I mean by that, that I had the unique privilege of being able to review documents that were produced by the organisation itself that conducted the activities, i.e., the Split Military District, subordinate units of the Split Military District, orders signed by, for example, General Gotovina, or by, for example, Generals Cermak or Markac, which is rarely the case in a traditional intelligence service because there one has rarely the original documents, and most of the times one has to work with sources who can be secondary or even third-hand or even fourth-hand. So the fact that I had first-hand sources, i.e., the original military documents was of course very interesting from the point of view of reliability of the sources. As to the credibility of the information, because of the volume whereby certain events were covered by not just one document but sometimes by ten, 15 documents or even more, and documents provided -- produced or provided by different originators, for example, one could have a report of an OG to the Split Military District Command about a certain event whereby at the same time there is report by the officer for intelligence and security, SIS, about the same event or even a report by the head of the department for political affairs again discussing the same event but from a different angle. That is, if I can express myself that way, almost an incredible luxury for an analyst in order to do his or her work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you ever faced with a situation where the documents gave contradictory information or did not allow for a clear conclusion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and this is visible in the second part of the report, when I discussed the relations, the professional relations between the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina, and the commander of the Knin garrison during and after Operation Storm, General Cermak. The documents, what I would call de facto documents, i.e., the documents that discuss the situation in August 1995 in Knin, did not allow me to draw a clear conclusion as to the subordination between or the subordination of Cermak to Gotovina as it prescribed in the doctrinal documents on garrison command which are reviewed in the first part of the report. And I have tried to describe the conclusions which I could draw on the situation which I -- where I stated the situation is not as clear-cut as one would expect from the doctrine. I have attempted to describe it as such in the second part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: During the course of your work, have you developed or formed any views about the authenticity of the documents or certain categories of these documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Obviously I'm not in a position to do any forensic investigation, because I -- I mean, I don't have the background and I only had copies to look at. But again applying the methodology I have explained, because of the fact that different sources would address the same event in a similar fashion, not only during the same time-period but sometimes there were, like, much reports from a later date, but again describing the same event in a similar fashion is important from the point of view of corroboration of the information. Also, an element of importance is that military documents have numbers, and, for example, the Office of the Prosecutor has the logs, the registers of these documents whereby, as it is in the case in the armies I'm familiar with, that a document when it is received is -- is recorded as incoming mail and when it is sent it is recorded as outgoing mail. I could compare that -- indeed the numbers I could find on the document were also available in these registers of incoming and outgoing mail. So these are some of the criteria I could apply to verify the authenticity of the documents I had access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have told us already yesterday, I believe, that you were not part of the investigation into the Gotovina case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you did not participate in any interviews of witnesses in the Gotovina case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now to finish off, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to go to the report itself and have the witness identify the structure. If we could pull up 65 ter 6098, please, and this is the report, the first part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now we'll see and I think we are all familiar with it, that it contains a cover page, then the next 14 pages is a table of contents. That's in e-court pages 2 to 14. Can you explain us the structure using the table of contents, in all briefness. We can all read it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the report has basically two parts. The first part is what I would call the de jure part, and that is intended to explain the basics of doctrine that existed in the Croatian armed forces at the time of the events, covering the aspects like structure, command and control within -- excuse me, command and control over the armed forces, i.e., the civilian command. Command and control within the armed forces, the planning and organisation of combat operations, as well as military discipline and military law. In the second part of the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we stop here for a moment. Before we go into the second part, in e-court pages 15 to 17, in the current document that's the first part, we see a section called scope. Can you explain what the purpose of the -- these couple of pages are?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the scope explains the overall structure of the report. Basically explains what I just mentioned for the first part of the report, and what I was about to mention for the second part of the report, and also mentions in brief terms the sources -- I mean, the categories of sources I used for the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page on e-court because that shows that scope part of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we move on to the next section. That's e-court page 18 through to 41. This is called executive summary, and we see now the first page. Can you explain the purpose of the executive summary and how it relates to the main body of your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the executive summary has two objectives. First of all, to summarize the key aspects of the report, and obviously following from that, the second objective is to present the -- the conclusions I drew from the material I reviewed. By conclusions I mean military conclusions, i.e., what was the significance of the different documents I reviewed and what did it mean from a military point of view. And as you may have noticed, I have tried for each -- and each section of the report starts with a summary, and -- which highlights the most important aspect of that section whereby the executive summary then summarizes the summaries of the individual sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, whether you want to mark for identification the first part of the report, or whether I should just move on to the next 65 ter, which is the second part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The report has been filed as a whole at the time. You want to split up now the two different --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The mere purpose is whether we should leave it as a 65 ter, hanging, or whether we should assign a marked for identification number, and indeed both parts can be together into one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact, it's preferable to have it marked for identification, if only that we have access to it in e-court. The Judges have no access to 65 ter numbers. And then since we're limited in the numbers of exhibits to have open on the screen, I would prefer to have the whole of the report under one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The second part would be 6099. If that could be brought up as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I'm asking you the following, Mr. Waespi, you earlier asked the CV to be admitted into evidence. Now I noticed that the CV is not mentioned in the filing in which the report was submitted. Neither is it mentioned in the table of contents of the report, but it is part of the filing. If we look at the page numbering, the sequential page numbering given by the registry in order to know what was filed. And then I see that a two-page CV, and the same, I think, as the one we admitted appears as the page numbers 3899 and 3900. The last one being the first page of the curriculum. And that's the same ERN number as the ERN number that was admitted a while ago. So now is it separate or is it also part of the report? It was part of the filing in which the report was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it is important and I understand that your decision, I think of the 18th December, addresses the qualifications of the expert based on this CV. So it is part of the report but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is part of the report, we can vacate the number that was assigned to the CV alone, and we would then have the expert report as submitted - when was it - in the filing of the 19th of December, 2007. That would then comprise the first part of the report, second part of the report, and the CV. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we vacate the number that was just assigned to the CV and that -- I wanted to say that we then assign that number to the whole of it, but, of course, the CV was admitted into evidence whereas it is suggested that the report is marked for identification only. So, therefore, perhaps it would be better to split that off because the CV is admitted, and I see no reason to change that at this moment, and then to assign the next number to the report, the two sections of it. Two 65 ter numbers, one exhibit number. Madam Registrar, what number would be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the report would be Exhibit number P1113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is marked for identification and keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You wanted to explain what the structure of the second part of the expert report was.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. So in the second part of the report, I focus on the events in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District between end of July and end of October 1995. In addition, I thought it would be useful also to explain -- to provide some background information, in relation to the existence of a self-declared Serb state in -- known as the RSK, as well as its armed forces. The deployment of an UN peacekeeping force in April 1992 and its mandate, and of course, also the relevant background elements in relation to the use of the special police inside and adjacent to the zone responsibility of the Split Military District during August 1995 and the command of the Knin garrison during and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter 6099 could be brought up, and that's a further complication, Mr. President. There is an addendum which is comprised of 42 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would then receive a -- for the time being, a separate number. So the report, one exhibit number; the addendum another exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I think in a -- my learned friend, I do believe that 6099 was part 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is part 2, at least what we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, it's 6101. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Theunens, why did you prepare an addendum.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the filing of the report in December 2007, I kept on conducting searches in the databases and in particular in the translation database to find out whether new documents that were relevant for my report had become available. In addition, Mr. Alan Tieger provided me with a hard copy of a list of documents the Prosecution wanted me to review, and I'm not sure anymore of the date, but I believe that was in April 2008. I reviewed the documents that were included in that list and then applied the same methodology as I did with the report in order to include documents I considered relevant, documents I had found myself or -- and/or that were included in the list into an addendum. I have mentioned in the introduction to the addendum, that the addendum includes documents that were obtained after December 2007. I want to clarify this, that I have also included a few documents that were available or that may have been available prior to December 2007, but when I did so, I did that because I considered it -- these older documents relevant, in order to provide additional background or explanation to the new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the addendum would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number P1114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And lastly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that -- yes, has the status of an exhibit -- of a document marked for identification and keeps that status for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, lastly, Mr. Theunens, if we could discuss 6151, please. Did you have a chance to review your report and draft a document called corrigendum?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did so. The corrigendum covers basically two aspects identified as contents and one -- and the second as footnotes, whereby I have attempted to identify all the typographic errors that were, unfortunately, still included in the version of the report that was filed in December 2007, as well as changes in translation. For example, one document, the war diary of the Split Military District which has been tender in the trial as P71, I was informed by, I think it was Mr. Morris or Mr. Shakhmetov that the initial translation was incomplete, and that the -- the amended or corrected translation was complete, which meant that all the references to page numbers of that document had to be reviewed, and if needed, corrected. And that can be seen in the footnotes section of the corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, since you're talking about corrigenda, you earlier said that you testified in the Seselj case and that that was new in February 2007. Was that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2008, Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to have this document marked for identification as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1115, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes my examination on the expertise of the witness and the methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, as I explained to you earlier, we've split up the portions of your evidence. We completed one portion yesterday. We're now in the second portion so the Defence will have an opportunity to cross-examine you on the matters that were raised until now by Mr. Waespi and on any other matter within this same area. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Preliminarily, Mr. Theunens, you said that Mr. Tieger give you a list of documents prior to your filing the addendum that we now have marked as P1114. Can you tell us how many documents he gave you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, the list had, I think, between 30 and 40 entries, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And approximately when was that that he gave you that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in April, but, again, because I work on several cases at the same time, it could also have been in March. But I understand that you have received a copy of that list and there is a date on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me go back it your CV, and you have a rank of Commandant coming out of the Belgian military forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What rank is that in the scheme of officer ranks within the Belgian military? Take us up from the lowest to the highest.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the rank between captain and major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is not my question. My question is take us from the lowest to the highest.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. We start at second lieutenant, I mean, from low. Then we have first lieutenant. Captain, commandant, major, lieutenant-colonel, colonel. We have brigadiers now but that is purely -- actually an administrative rank which is only applied in international organisations. Then we have major-generals, lieutenant-generals, and we have two generals, i.e., the chief of Defence Staff has four stars, as well as the king who is a supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, during your military career you -- well, what was the largest unit that you ever commanded?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest -- I mean, do you mean unit -- sorry. Do you mean largest by manpower or by equipment or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By manpower.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, really command was -- I was the acting commander of a company during an exercise, a tank company, which is approximately 80 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in that circumstance you were the acting commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Putting aside your acting commanding over 80 people, what is the largest unit of men over which you had full command as the superior?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, full -- I mean, an acting commander has full command because otherwise is he not a commander. And, yeah, so the position I held before, platoon commander, I was responsible for 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So you were a platoon commander and responsible for 15 people, and when you were an acting commander you were responsible for 80, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's when you are a tank company commander that -- or acting tank company commander you are responsible for 80 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us go through some of your military background, sir, and I would like to address ourselves to -- by the way, before I do that, how long were you an acting commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the longest period in -- the longest was for one or two weeks but it happened at several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So -- and how many occasions did that happen in?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think three or four. The situation was that the company commander was attending French language courses, which is one of the mandatory things in a -- for a person who has Dutch as a mother tongue and vice versa, before attending the second level staff course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And it's fair to say that any of these positions that you held were being held during peacetime and not during a time of war. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. But if you allow me, I would like to explain that -- or I would like to add that peace or war, the principles are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn our attention to your education. I mean, you noted for us several times on direct examination some of the courses that you took in military history and military sciences, and you also took physics and chemistry and psychology. Now, you would not consider yourself an expert in all these different disciplines would you, simply because you took a course in the Military Academy in those items?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it is up to me to determine whether I am expert or not. I can talk about my professional experience and explain why I believe that my experience, both the educational or academic as well as professional experience, is relevant for the report, but I don't think it is up to me to determine whether I am an expert or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, my question to you is: Do you believe that you are an expert in those disciplines simply because you took a course in them?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is I do not believe -- I mean, the answer is that whether or not a person is an expert because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Do you have a difficulty understanding my question? I'm asking whether you believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Mr. Kehoe would like to know, I think, Mr. Theunens, whether on the basis of the courses you followed in other matters, whether you would consider yourself an expert in these fields. The first question is: Have you ever considered that for yourself, whether you would be an expert in chemistry, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, chemistry was not my strongest course, I have to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Join the club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my question simply was whether you ever considered the question for yourself whether you are an expert in chemistry, which I understand for some lawyers is not an easy one, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, what you are pointing at. Obviously I never considered myself an expert in chemistry or any specific course I took because, in my understanding of the word "expertise," it is not just a matter of academic qualifications, it's also a matter of professional experience and if you wish I can explain that further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Kehoe wants further explanation, he will certainly ask for it. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us be more direct on that score, Mr. Theunens, and talk to you a bit about artillery and your expertise in the field of artillery. You told us yesterday and, Your Honours and my learned friends, it's at page 12179, beginning on line 5, and if at any point you want me it read back verbatim what it says, Mr. Theunens, I will do so, that you took a ballistic course. Now this ballistics course that you took was in the academy, was it not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, and that was the first element of my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then during -- when you were a commissioned officer, I believe, and this at line 9 on that same page, you noted that you took a week-long forward observer school, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a forward observer school is -- is just training what a forward observer does with artillery saying, Look, you know, you got to go so far to the left or so far to the right. That's what it does, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's basically what I recall from the course. I mean, obviously there is background information on the types of fire, the different command and control relations that exist between the unit that provides the fire support and the unit requests the support. But in practical terms it is as you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think the last item that you gave us in that score was - and this begins on same page, Your Honours, line 21 - a brigade level staff course where you learned the use of many different weapons during a year-long course, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I mentioned, that also included the organisation of artillery support on brigade level which I consider very significant in the scope of the matters related to the artillery I addressed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You never commanded an artillery group either at a corps or a division or a brigade level, have you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now is it a fact, sir, that are you not an expert in artillery, are you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a correct observation, Your Honours, and I have not tried to create such an impression in my report. In my report, I have not addressed the technical issues, i.e., whether or not the right targets were engaged, and if there was collateral damage or undesired damage, whether or not that could be statistically explained. That is it not a field of my expertise and I have therefore not endeavoured to express any professional conclusions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you not, in your report, Mr. Theunens, offer an opinion that the artillery attack on Knin and other towns in the Krajina were indiscriminately fired upon? Did you not offer that opinion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you direct me to the page where I make that opinion or express that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you pull up the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On page 180, and I believe this is part 2.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I have written there is that -- I wiil read out the sentence: "The duties of the Split Military District artillery include," and then I open the parenthesis, meaning that I'm quoting from a document which has been actually been addressed at an earlier stage in the report, "putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac and Gracac under artillery fire and then I add myself without indicating which specific targets in Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire." And then I add myself: "Without indicating which specific targets in Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac the Split Military District artillery is to engage." I have not used the expression "indiscriminate." I have -- all I have tried to do is to quote from the order. I then compared that order with what I had learned in my brigade level staff course, where we would -- for each and every target have a precise description. I understand that the Croatian armed forces did not use the same grid reference system as we did, but at least there would be a description like the command post or that enemy battalion or the logistics centre. I mean, a specific identification of the target which goes beyond the level of the name of a smaller or bigger town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing to read the portion after you stopped.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The fact that the orders of subordinate units, the OG Zadar order for the attack of artillery dated 3 August 1995 instructs: 'Put the following towns under artillery fire, Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, that were reviewed during the preparation of this report do not contain more specific targeting information either.'" And this is your opinion: "Suggests that the Split Military District commander and its subordinate commands regard these Serb-controlled towns as military targets that could be engaged with artillery." You support that on the next page, page 181, where you cite an order or a report by Brigadier Ademi back to General Gotovina where it says: "This conclusion is reinforced by a report," and you gave the report number, Brigadier Rahim Ademi, Chief of Staff of the Split Military District and commander OG, Operative Group, of course, Livno, sends on 7 May 1995 to Major-General Gotovina, commander of the Split Military District. Ademi informs Gotovina in this report that: "Pursuant to your command, we are ready to open fire on Knin within four hours. Ademi's report to Gotovina does not mention which military targets are to be engaged." Now, Mr. Theunens, by the inclusion of those paragraphs in your report, you were attempting to suggest to the Chamber that Knin, certainly Obrovac, Benkovac, Gracac, and by logical conclusion Knin was fired upon indiscriminately, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that that is a correct representation of what I have written. But before going to the issue of your question, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to 65 ter 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Excuse me. Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness started what -- to answer the question and he thought that relevant for his answer was to draw our attention to a certain document and the witness is entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On page 185, I quote from the operative log-book of the 4th Guards Brigade, which is one of the Guards Brigades of the Split Military District. This document is 65 ter 4581. And I have included some entries which I considered relevant in the context of the use of artillery by the Split Military District during Operation Storm on page 185, and, for example, the last entry I quoted for the 4th of August, dated -- 1038 hours, I will read it out : "Brigade commander asks not to pound Knin anymore since our troops are already there." The reason I mentioned this is that, as I tried to explain when I addressed the methodology, one should not look at documents in isolation. Secondly, to address the question you asked, basic -- I have not made an analysis of use of artillery -- I mean, of whether or not Knin was shelled or not. All I have done is used the information included in orders by Gotovina and his subordinate units as well as you read out an earlier note or report by his Chief of Staff where the possibility of shelling these towns is being addressed. Now I have read out an entry in the diary of the 4th Guards Brigade, indicating that indeed Knin was shelled or was -- was exposed to artillery fire. I have nowhere suggested whether or not Knin was shelled indiscriminately. I think that's an important distinction between what is in the report and what you tried to -- to present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, let's take first things first. Let us look at the page that you looked at, on page 185, where it talks about ceasing firing on Knin. That is an order to cease firing on the Knin area because HV troops are in town, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, 1038, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now go back to page 180. Is it your testimony now that, on page 180, the bottom of that page, and your supporting paragraph on the next page, 181, where you discuss the piece of information that was sent by Brigadier Ademi to General Gotovina. Is it your testimony that you, based on that information, were not trying to suggest to this Chamber that towns in the Krajina were indiscriminately fired upon pursuant to the order of General Gotovina. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the question has been answered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, certainly the witness had not said yes or no. Whether this is a yes or no answer could still be seen. But did you -- could you please clarify what your position is in relation to this question. If can you do it by yes or no, fine; if you think you couldn't, then please give us the answer, but a brief answer is preferred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will try to be brief, even though it will not be a yes or no answer. What I have stated in the report is that the artillery of the Split Military District can engage these municipalities. Whether or not they did, I did not have the information available to determine which targets they engaged and that was not in the scope of my report. So I think there's an important distinction between what they could do and what they actually did. My report addresses what they could do, and for what they actually did, I only have the entries in the diary of the 4th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that if you say the report tells us what they could do, that what you wanted to express is that on the basis of the documents you found, what limits on what they could do were found in those documents and that you expressed that in your report. Is that a more precise formulation of what they could do, because what someone can do is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. So I mentioned in the report what the view of the commander of the Split Military District was in relation to the shelling of Knin based on the deployment of his weapons and his -- the planning he had in order to conduct his part of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I just may follow up, Mr. President, on your question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then what were you suggesting to the Trial Chamber when you said that this particular order, they do not contain more specific targeting information. What were you suggesting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I answered the question, Your Honours, but I can repeat it. That based on my expertise in planning of artillery fire, on one hand, as well as documentation from the Split Military District I reviewed, I would have expected more detailed information as to which specific targets were to be engaged in these towns. I have included examples of the kind of targeting information one would expect on page 187 of my report where -- and that is exactly the same as I learned in my military. We have a number for the target, there is a -- a description of the target with coordinates, as well as a physical description of the target and identification of who can engage the target. One doesn't have to be an artillery expert to know that this is the basic information that is required in order to allow those that have to carry out the fire to know what they have to fire on when. Now, maybe these lists exists for Knin, Benkovac and Drvar, but I would have expected, again, based on my background, that such information would have been included in the order, or that at least the description would be much more specific than, as we read out in the beginning, the town of Knin, the town of Benkovac, Drvar, and Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I take you have not been shown some of those targeting documents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether -- it could be that in the lists I received from Mr. Tieger in April that there were such lists included, but the lists, for example, I included on page 187 is something -- yes, is one of the documents or one of the relevant documents in this context I've -- I found doing the searches, and this specific one addresses targets to be engaged by units -- artillery units of the Split Military District. So when I had the information, I included it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you did get lists of targets from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I'm sorry for the transcript. I made my own searches. So I may have received some documents from the Office of the Prosecutor, but in addition, I did my own searches. So it is not just a matter of receiving documents, it is also a matter of identifying the documents myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer to the question is that -- we'll get back to this issue at some length in any event. But going back to your expertise, your collecting of those documents and the -- your actual exercise of collecting these documents in conjunction with your background does not render you an expert in artillery, does it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that I have answered the question. I'm not an artillery expert. I have not pretended to be one. But I do believe that my military training and expertise allow me to draw the conclusions I drew in my report as to the planning or -- and the choice of targets which is indicated in the reports that we just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. I just wanted to be clear that you are not, in fact, an artillery expert. Now, given your rank in -- given your rank and your experience in the Belgian military, and you told us that you had never had any experience in high-level command and control, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday I answered a similar question by Mr. Waespi in the sense that, indeed, I did not exercise that command and control myself. But I worked in the staffs, both the General Staff of the Belgian armed forces, doing an exercise in a brigade staff, as well as the force command of significant peacekeeping operations, both UN-led as well as a combined joint task force which was kind of NATO-led later on. So I believe that I'm in a position to understand how command and control works at whatever level and how it is being implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you -- your own -- and I'm directing this towards you personally: Do you consider yourself an expert in high-level command and control issues?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider, Your Honours, that I'm able to discuss and provide professional conclusions on the issues I have addressed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not my question, sir. My question, quite simply, and I will read it back to you again, is: Do you consider yourself an expert in high-level command and control issues?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then I would like to know what criteria am I to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's see -- let me go back to something else and you can tell me what criteria you applied because what we'll do is, we will bring up 1D62-0001. And what this is, is it's the draft article that you talked to us about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there has not been a translation of this to date, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But this is the draft article that you wrote, Mr. Theunens, the role of military expertise in laying and defending criminal charges. You recognise that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is the article that you were discussing yesterday on direct examination with my learned friend? Yes? You have to --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 6 of this document. Under the heading, Role of military expertise during the trial phase. If we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just want to give you the reference point in this, Mr. Theunens, so when we talk about implementation -- if we just scroll that up a little bit. And you note that the OTP generally calls two types of military experts, external military experts and internal or in-house military experts. External military experts are specialists in particular military aspects of a case which require detailed technical knowledge and expertise, like, for example artillery, sniper or logistics experts. Now artillery. You recognise that the Office of the Prosecutor has retained an outside expert for artillery issues, do you not? In this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next portion which we were talking about. Other external experts that you describe in your article. Senior officers with high-level command and control experience and in brackets you have brigadier, commander or more senior, and preferably operational experience in a zone of conflict. Now in your article, why did you say that you're looking for somebody at a -- excuse me, a brigade commander rank or higher to discuss high-level command and control issues? Why did you include that in your article?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my article tries to describe my experiences -- I mean, the experiences or the things I have seen being done in the ICTY and in a number of trials, depends a bit of the nature of the trial, but I'm familiar with trials where both Prosecution as well as Defence called a General to testify on very specific command and control issues whereby this -- this General would address, again, very specific issues, not referring to the volume or not being -- basing himself on the volume of material I reviewed in order to address a very specific command and control aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, Mr. Theunens, that the reason why a senior officer needs to be called is because you wrote that you want somebody with high-level command and control experience. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not determine who the Prosecutor calls or not. I believe that the approach that is -- that has existed in -- what has been applied in a number of trials, i.e., that have you a General who comes and explains how it should have been, on that command level, together with an in-house analyst who is hired -- who is asked to review the material is an efficient approach but that is just my personal observation. Again, I do not determine who is being called by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you are here to address command and control issues in your report, do you know why the Office of the Prosecutor is calling a separate expert or has a separate expert on their witness list to address command and control issues? Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the logical answer would be that you better ask the person who decides about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us continue on here, that we've established that you were not a senior officer, that you don't have high-level command and control experience, and that you have not had operational experience in a zone of conflict, have you? And the operative word there is "operational experience" in a zone of conflict. Maybe you can explain to the Chamber what you first meant by operation and then explain why you don't have it.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I am confused because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read -- go back to your article. When you're looking for an expert -- you write in your article, when you're looking for an expert to talk about command and control issues, you're looking for a high-level command and control senior officer preferably with operational experience in a zone of conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first ask the witness, because I think that was part of his earlier answer. Have you expressed in this article what your wishes would be if you would be in charge of conducting a trial or have you described here, that's at least how I read it, what is done by the OTP in the ICTY? That's how I read it. Mr. Kehoe, earlier you said you want this and you want that. I refrained from commenting at that moment. But let's be clear on what the witness describes here. That is apparently a practice in which he observes and this is the only part I've read. So I have not read the whole of it. So if there's anywhere else, then please lay a foundation for whether this is what the witness would do. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I might have a minute. Yes, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The difficulty, Your Honour -- and I go back to the answer by Mr. Theunens about why certain things are done a certain way, Mr. Theunens responded that I should go ask the OTP. And, that of course, is somewhat circular given the fact that he is saying that is in fact how it should be done when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He doesn't say how it should be done. He says what is done. That's what he describes here, isn't it? Is there anything this is what the OTP should do or does it say what is usually done? Which is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not -- let's focus on. Refraining from any further comments, I just want you to be very precise on what -- on the basis of what you show at this moment to the witness and that is the only thing the Chamber sees to -- to refrain from telling the witness what he wants, where he describes what is done, that if the witness says, This is done, the why, please ask those who make these decisions, that is not to avoid an answer. That is not part of this article. The witness does not describe what should be done but what is is done. At least that is what I read at this moment, and your question is based -- apparently on a different understanding. And if there is a possibility that one would disagree on what is written there, then we should first of all seek clarification from the witness, what he intended to describe here. Whether it's normative or whether it is a description of what is the practice what is usually done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And going back to my earlier question, Mr. Theunens, do you know the reason why the OTP retained outside experts on, for instance, command and control issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I object. What is the relevancy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness would know then he could tell us. What, then, for conclusions to draw is a different matter. If you know why the Prosecution acts, as you describe it does, please explain to us what the basis of your knowledge and explain why they do it. If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Also to clarify the previous question, there is a footnote number mentioned at the end of the sentence that was quoted by Mr. Kehoe. It's footnote 36. And if we scroll down in e-court, we will indeed see that this observation I make is based on what has been done in a number of other trials, like the Strugar trial, Hadzihasanovic, and so on and so on. To come back now to the last question, and that can actually be found on the next page of the article, that is that on the one hand, again based on my observations, the OTP wishes to introduce military evidence in an organised and an efficient manner, in order to facilitate the Trial Chamber's task in evaluating that material, my understanding again from looking at a number of trials and my own experience in this organisation, is that in-house analysts can be used for that purpose. In addition to that, the Office of the Prosecutor also considers it's useful that in some military trials use is made of external experts in the area of technical expertise, like artillery or sharpshooter, as well as command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question, sir, and I will go back to it, is: Do you know the reasons why the OTP retains outside experts, for instance, for command and control issues? The question was why, not the fact that they do it. Why?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to be impolite. But it's -- I think the Senior Trial Attorney together with his trial attorneys determines which witness to call and what evidence to present, and they're better placed than me to determine why or not a witness, including external command and control experts, should be called or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your conversations with the Senior Trial Attorneys for the OTP, have they discussed with you that you did not have the qualifications to render an expert opinion on high-level command and control issues and that was the reason why they hired an outside expert?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are two questions, Mr. Theunens. The first one is whether it has been discussed with you that you did not have the qualification to render expert opinion on high-level command and control issues. Was that discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that was not discussed, was it communicated to you what the reason was that the OTP would hire an outside expert, apparently on those matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These motives were not explained to me or these reasons were not explained to me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to go into a different issue. I don't know if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think then we first should have a break. After the break, Mr. Russo, you will be the first one to address the Court. How much time, I earlier asked three or five minutes but if you want to choose for four or six, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I feel I can do it in three to five, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00. Mr. Theunens, you're not expected back -- two times five minutes, ten minutes. You can arrive a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Russo, the Chamber has considered how much time it would grant to the Defence on the matter we are dealing with at this moment, and the Chamber came to the conclusion that the same time as Mr. Waespi took on expertise and methodology should be given to the Defence, and then for the Defence as a whole. I don't know whether you discussed among yourselves which Defence team would deal with what. From the history, it appears that the Cermak Defence has not addressed the matter of qualification in -- last January. The Markac has joined whatever the Gotovina Defence had raised in relation to the qualifications of the witness. The Chamber has, therefore, considered the positions taken by the parties in the past. The Chamber has also considered the way in which the cross-examination is conducted at this moment and came to the conclusion and we still need the exact time that for the Defence as a whole, that the same time would be available -- as Mr. Waespi took. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Without interrupting, Your Honour, just one matter. I was going to be dealing with these matters in my cross-examination of this witness because I considered it a matter at large in to these matters that the Court is addressing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course we should make a difference between the qualifications as an expert whether or not we could accept the report or whether it could be considered to be an expert report, and of course another matter is whether an expert has drawn solid conclusions on the basis of the material he had or whether, perhaps, he had not all the material available which, of course, would be in part of the cross-examination. This is not any way to suggest that parties would be excluded to address the issue of methodology or expert knowledge in relation to the elements of the, report but, of course, what we did, until now, is we dealt with it on a rather general basis, although now and then an example arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can deal with the issues, in fact, now rather than later. It makes more sense to me, now that we're dealing with it this way, to put my issues before the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are issues of a general nature and if they're different from what the Gotovina Defence has raised and will raise, then, of course, we -- the Chamber has considered the matter on the basis of what submissions were made in the past. And there were no specific submissions in which the -- at least by the Cermak Defence, no specific submissions saying he does not qualify as an expert which seems to be one of the central issues in the Gotovina Defence's submissions, and joined by the Markac Defence. So I -- we'll consider --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether -- of course if you want to raise issues of expert knowledge, qualifications, but not to say he doesn't qualify as an expert to present the report, but the way he has done his work is not good or should be challenged or on the basis of insufficient material which he was insufficiently aware of, that of course are matters which are not a direct attack to the qualifications of Mr. Theunens as an expert and there, of course, there is a different position by the Cermak Defence compared to the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Methodology we always viewed as being a rather different matter, and being phase two, we're dealing with both matters at this stage, but methodology was something that we were very conscious of as being a matter to be addressed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and methodology is not a matter which is specifically mentioned in 94 bis where only the qualifications of the witness as such are mentioned, where the parties are expected to express themselves. We will further consider, but we want to put limits to the time especially on the qualifications as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm crossing off issues that I would have raised any way that Mr. Kehoe has dealt with, but there are other matter that may still not be addressed by him which could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, of course it would be appreciated -- I don't have the exact time at this moment the time Mr. Waespi -- you took, Mr. Waespi. The registry is preparing the relevant data for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just on the timing score, and I appreciate the Chamber's concerns regarding timing, and I have consulted with my learned friend Mr. Kay to avoid that duplication, and we -- during the break we've agreed that I was not going to into something because he said that he was going to go into it, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now, Mr. Waespi has taken 1 hour and 44 minutes, dealing with these matter, well, let's say the second subject. And you have used until now, Mr. Kehoe, 45 minutes on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, I think I will deal with a topic that wouldn't be dealt by Mr. Kehoe or by Mr. Kay. This is the topic of the special police and therefore I will need, let's say, around ten minutes on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps we -- let's be very practical. How much still -- how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, I think I would probably need at most 15 minutes and then I'm not discussing the discipline issue on that score, which is Mr. Misetic's issue and I think he has got 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than half an hour. Mr. Kay, could you give us -- if you want do raise any methodology of a general character at this moment, how much time you would need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I could deal with my matters in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In 20 minutes. And Mr. Mikulicic, you said you would need ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. That approximately fills the hour which would, on the basis of what the Chamber in mind would still be available to the Defence but now split up among the various Defence teams. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Given the pace at which events transpired yesterday and the Court's ultimate decision to ask Mr. Theunens to produce the draft reports of his expert report, the OTP is seeking some clarification on the Chamber's position. It's the OTP's understanding that the Court's position was expressed in two areas. The first being that the OTP does not have an obligation to disclose drafts of expert reports, which, of course, we're not taking issue with. The second position was that a party who retains an expert to prepare a report for trial has no claim or propriety interest over the drafts of that expert if the expert themselves are willing to provide the reports. In other words, irrespective of any claim that could be made by the party retaining the expert, that the expert themselves have the right to produce the report if they wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first deal with the first one. OTP does not have an obligation to disclose drafts of expert reports which were not taken issue with. The Chamber has not ruled on any obligation to disclose, as a matter of fact, since this witness has -- has told the Chamber that he has no problems whatsoever to share previous versions of his expert report with whomever, I would say, as a matter of fact, that the motion filed is moot and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will withdraw it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll withdraw it. So there is no ruling on that. Yesterday you may remember, Mr. Russo, that the Chamber said that on the basis of what was presented, that the Chamber decided that it could not give an order to disclose. And that might give you some clue as that it may depend quite a bit, on many circumstances, whether, at a certain moment, there would be a duty to disclose. On the basis of what we heard yesterday, the Chamber could not conclude that there was such an obligation, which would have resulted in an order by the Chamber to disclose that material. Now, that's the first area. You said the second position was that a party who retains an expert to prepare a report for trial has no claim or propriety interest over the drafts of that expert and you said if the expert themselves are willing to provide the reports. In other words, irrespective of any claim could be made by the party retaining the expert, that the expert themselves have to try to produce -- it's not entirely clear what you meant in the second point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the OTP's understanding the Court sought from the witness whether the witness would have any difficulty in providing the drafts of his report, the witness indicated that he wouldn't have any difficulty doing that and the Court subsequently asked him to that. The Court's question to the witness of whether or not he would and then the subsequent request that he do produce the draft reports presupposes that the witness has the right and/or authority to, in fact, give that report to the Court. That was my intention, that seeking clarification of the fact that it is the position of the Chamber that irrespective of any claim that the Prosecution may wish to make that the expert has a right, in and of himself, to offer that report to whom he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My position would be that we're now in the realm of hypotheticals because, with all due respect, I don't think it is an issue that we can make a blanket statement about all experts. There is -- this is a quite -- an area of the law that there may be an issue with non-testifying experts, for example, that are retained by one side or the other, not for the purpose of testifying in the trial, where a party may in fact have a right to preclude the expert from surrendering something to the other side. So before we get into, really, hypothetical situations that later on could be used for whatever purpose, I think it might be wise at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Unless we're talking about on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we could -- but I have to consider that with my colleagues. Apparently the issue Mr. Russo raises is whether a party by inviting an expert, ask him to write a report, whether that party is in a position to prohibit the expert to give earlier versions of his report if he himself has no problem in providing these earlier versions. So whether there is such a level of control by the party who hires an expert who, of course, still is independent because he will form his opinion on the basis of his -- of his qualifications as an expert and not on the basis of instructions, as far as the content is concerned, by the party that hires him. And I think the matter you wanted to raise is whether a party can say, I hired this expert. The expert is willing to give an earlier version but now I, party A or party B, I now tell this expert that he couldn't do that, and from what I understand is that you would deny such a power by the party that has hired that expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, we're seeking the Court's clarification that that is in fact the Court's position, and if it is, that it would clearly apply to both parties and we would be, certainly, happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider. I'm not making any further observations on the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- although I think I could -- I think I said yesterday a few things that might even complicate matters a bit more than --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as it stands in accordance with the -- how you presented it. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I again -- I think that there's no written motion pending and the underlying facts aren't clear.
