And there is an issue that has not yet been discussed in front of the Chamber with respect to another witness, so I would like to avoid the situation where the Trial Chamber says, for example, we can contact the witness independently to try to get the drafts and that that might somehow later be used as an argument that the OTP then wouldn't have an obligation to produce it themselves to the extent they had it. So, without getting into all sorts of different hypothetical scenarios, I suggest that we work out amongst ourselves the issue with respect to the next expert witness to come, and if there is a problem, then the party can file a written motion and ask for relief from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course Mr. Russo is always entitled to seek guidance from the Chamber, but preferably to be done in a written submission. I see now what you apparently are seeking. There are, as I said, the matter may be even a bit more complex than you presented it. Then of course, the Defence will have an opportunity to respond. Another way of dealing with the matter is that -- not to seek guidance but just to head for the next expert and see where we are with that expert. But I leave it up to you whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's no matter, then I would like Mr. Theunens to be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I would seek permission to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course you are, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we'll continue. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'd like to talk you about your part 1 of your report which is your -- you described it as the de jure portion of your report. And I believe you described, and I don't have the exact terminology, as a compilation of laws and regulations from the Republic of Croatia as well as the Croatian army. Is that accurate on a general level?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you, yourself, have never studied law, have you, other than taking a course at the academy?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe that you need a law degree to understand things like a constitution or Law on Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I asked you a question. I asked you have you studied law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ... Yes. The question was whether you never studied law, have you, other than taking a course at the academy. This question allows you to, first of all, tell us whether you had -- whether you followed any other courses apart from the course you took at the academy; and, second, also allows you to explain to us whether in any other way you familiarized yourself with matters directly related to the law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I described yesterday as the course in law covered several years, so there was law in the first year, second year, third year, and fourth year. And also in staff course we -- the brigade level course, we had courses on law of armed conflict, so I believe I am qualified to analyse constitutions, defence laws and related legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, are you not a legal expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, a defence law, a constitution is intended for the citizens of a country. A defence law is intended for military personnel, in particular for officers. I don't expect that all the citizens of a country have a law degree, but still they are supposed to understand the constitution. The same applies to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kehoe. You are asking -- by these questions you are asking for these kind of answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are, Mr. Kehoe. The witness is entitled to answer the question, although if you could keep it brief ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. My understanding is it that a defence law is intended for military personnel and that at least the officers, whatever their educational background may be, are in a position to understand the obligations and duties that are established by the defence law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can show you a piece of your testimony, sir, of -- that you gave in the Martic case at page 1011, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could show it via Sanction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On line 18, did you tell the Martic Chamber that: "I am not a legal expert"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's indeed -- that is what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's a fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is as it is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you made a decision on laws to include in your report and not include in your report even though you have no legal expertise. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is that I made a selection of laws and regulations, then the answer is correct, I made such a selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you made that selection without being a legal expert, and after you made that selection of laws, you then applied facts to those laws to write your report. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I tried to explain, it is my view that one doesn't have to be a legal expert in order to understand a constitution or a defence law and in order to analyse to what extent these legal provisions were applied or not during a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, suffice it to say, the Trial Chamber should just get a bundle of these documents that are selected as well as any supporting material and it is up to the expertise of the Trial Chamber, as opposed to your commentary, to make that assessment of the applicability of those laws to those facts. Isn't that the way the Trial Chamber should be handling this situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I do not expect the witness to tell this Court how it should handle certain issues. Let me remind you that at various, various, various occasions legal texts were put to witnesses who, from what we know of those witnesses, certainly had far less legal education, legal experience, nevertheless, they were asked without any hesitation to tell us what it meant, what the implications were, et cetera, et cetera. Now this witness has explained to us what courses he took in law and also explained to us some knowledge in specific fields of law and then to say, Are you a legal expert? That's the same as to ask someone, Are you an expert in music? And then he will say, I am or I'm not, depending on whether he plays piano or flute, because he is not an expert in playing the flute. And if you would have asked Arthur Rubenstein whether he was a very good piano player he might denied that. Others would not. That means that it's a matter of judgement to some extent, what this Chamber is interested in, to know on what -- how the witness developed knowledge, skills or experience which allows him to assist the Chamber in better understanding certain matters. And that is not by saying, Are you a legal expert? It's a yes or no, that is a simplification which is not -- is not substantially assisting the Chamber in making the judgement on whether it should or should not accept the assistance of an expert who offers his skills, his knowledge or his experience to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate your guidance, Mr. President. I merely address paragraph 29 of Your Honours' -- of the Chamber's ruling, where Your Honour wanted a delineation of matters that were opinions offered by the witness as opposed to fields of expertise. And I take it from paragraph 29, as it plays into paragraph 25, that there was a clear demarcation in the Chamber's mind between those two areas, and that was the reason I was exploring. I understand that pieces -- that items have been given to other witnesses for explanation and I would assume, absent a specific expertise in many cases, that will be rendered to be an opinion or a position of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore it is certainly important to know whether Mr. Theunens specialized in the law of taxation or other legal matters in the past, but to say, Are you a legal expert is so broad. Let not spend more time on this. You may continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I was merely addressing that particular matter, but to go into this particular area more specifically, and we are talking about the area of discipline, I will turn it over to Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens,

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, with respect to military discipline, have you ever published anything on the topic of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The only thing I did outside of, obviously, my duties as an officer was that a couple of months ago I gave a lecture in the OTP to interns on the role of the military in establishing the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But that topic didn't deal specifically with the issue of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you consult literature on the role of the military in relation to establishing the rule of law, you will -- one of the first things that every -- whether it is academicians or a professional officer will comment, is that only disciplined forces can be used to establish the rule of law, and that, therefore, an understanding of military discipline is quite essential in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you -- in addition to this seminar for interns have you ever lectured or otherwise spoken in public about the issue of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke very often -- I'm sorry for the transcript. I spoke very often to my soldiers when I was a platoon commander as well as to my officer cadets about the importance of discipline and why they had to do certain things, which, at first glance, didn't seem pleasant or appropriate or agreeable in their view, and obviously that was related to the enforcement of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking more about in an academic or professional capacity. Have you lectured or spoken in public on the issue of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to your role as a platoon commander, do you have any specific knowledge about military discipline that the average Belgian platoon commander doesn't have?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would hope that all officers, be it Belgian or for whatever country, have an understanding of military discipline, but I have no particular talents in that area that anybody else have. To the extent that I can judge the knowledge of my fellow officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us or identify any texts within the last ten years that you have read that deal primarily with the issue of military discipline. And I'm not talking about texts that relates to the issue; I'm talking about texts that primarily deal with the issue of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will find a number of footnotes in my report that deal with that issue. For example, I think FM 100-5, the US regulation operations, addresses the concept of disciplined operations. It is addressed in Part 7 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I should have been more specific. I'm talking about academic studies, academic publications, law review articles, anything in the area of academia dealing primarily with the issue of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that I believe that because we have a different background that my answer will be -- I mean, is obviously different. I don't expect to find -- I'm sorry, I will rephrase it. My understand it that I prefer to read a military regulation on military discipline instead of an academic article because my experience is that military regulations are much more practical and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, may I stop you there. The question that was put to you was a very factual question, whether you had read material over the last ten years, if Mr. Kehoe [sic] would like that know what you may have read instead and whether you considered it to be more -- a better use of your time to read other things is another matter. The question was a very factual one. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I object to being confused with Mr. Misetic. I'm much better looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Not as much as I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see how alert our transcriber is who said [sic]. So it learns as how we can rely on those assisting us. I will give it some more nights of sleep. It is a good or a bad thing for you, Mr. Kehoe, to be addressed as Mr. Misetic or for you, Mr. Misetic, to be addressed as Mr. Kehoe. I, however, would like to be addressed as the Presiding Judge. If there is no confusion about that. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I apologise for the initial digression. In order to prepare this lecture on the rule of law, I did indeed read a number of articles which were published, for example, in the US Military Review. There were also articles from Parameters, which is another American military magazine which is intended for mainly senior officers. And I haven't checked the material before coming here, but if you want I can bring it for the next break. There are academic articles on the aspect of the importance of military discipline in relation to the enforcement of the rule of law by military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, if could you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. President, if could I ask that the witness provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness is willing to bring them, that would be appreciated, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would just imply, Your Honours, that I am allowed to go to my office during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may fetch them at your office. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when is the first time that you began to study the Croatian Code of military discipline from 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time must have been in -- the first time must have been in January 2007. Right after receiving the tasking for the compilation of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you get any assistance from anyone in interpreting the Croatian Code or is that strictly your interpretation of the Code based on your reading?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive assistance from others in -- for me when reading the -- and interpreting and analysing the 1992 Code of Discipline, Croatian Code of Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Croatia and do your own investigation of the Croatian archives to find documents on the issue of military -- Croatian military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not, Your Honours. And I can explain if you want why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- if Mr. Misetic is interested to hear your explanation, and he apparently is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my position whereby the Prosecution team had asked me to compile a report, it was also made clear that I would not part of the investigation and that if I had certain requirements in relation to documents, I could express them towards the two military intelligence analysts working on the case. And that is what I did. And I mentioned an example yesterday. During my searches I did not come across a specific Croatian military regulation dealing with the implementation or the international laws of war. And that was one of the questions I raised with my two colleagues because they were going to the archives or were participating in the drafting of requests for assistance to the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say then that your understanding of Croatian military discipline is limited to the documents that are actually in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I wish to add that when I reviewed decisions on military discipline to impose disciplinary measures or sentences or appeals there -- the reference were always made or there were often references made to the code of discipline and that was actually the code I was reviewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to -- and you correct me if I'm wrong, but if I understood you correctly yesterday, where there were gaps in the documentation of the Office of the Prosecutor on Croatian law, you turned to other sources to try to reconstruct that specific area of the law, for example, the law of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or US military law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would replace the word "law" by "military regulations," and then the observation is correct. I quoted from SFRY law on All People's Defence maybe in introduction but not as a replacement for Croatian law. I did quote from SFRY armed forces regulations as well as US military regulations when there was a gap, but also to show the universal character of the Croatian military regulations I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And finally, where you used SFRY or US regulations to fill in gaps, in some cases those gaps are because there was no Croatian law at the time, and in other cases it's because there may have been another Croatian law but you didn't have access do it. Is that correct? I'm sorry, regulation. I stike the law part. So let me rephase the question. Where there were gaps, you filled those -- those gaps, from your perspective, could have been either because there was no Croatian regulation on that point or there was a Croatian regulation but you didn't access to it in the Office of the Prosecutor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you will now be cross-examined on this issue by Mr. Kay, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A few details, first of all, please, Mr. Theunens. When was the date that you started your work on this case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, in December 2006, but I don't remember the exact date. I had an informal meeting with Douglas Marks Moore and Alan Tieger about possible support to this case, and then in January, I started -- I mean, we discussed the 10- and the 17-point taskings. I started to work on the report. My work in this case is limited to the work on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that would be from January 2007.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at documentation that you were given, were you given a copy of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not given a copy of the indictment but I decided myself to read the indictment just to understand the time-frame, the events, and other issues I considered relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned the Defence pre-trial briefs. Did you see the Prosecution pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked again the documents on my desk last evening and indeed had a copy of the Defence pre-trial brief which I read, and also a copy of the Office of the Prosecutor pre-trial brief, but I have no precise recollection to what extent I read the last document. I remember reading the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us you were part of the military analyst team and that's the group that you work with in the Office of the Prosecutor, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation as developed over the years,Your Honours, initially -- and we are still on paper a team but in fact each analyst is assigned to a trial team, whereby we may talk to each other, of course, in order to learn from each other's experience, but I must say that my interaction with the other members of the team was rather limited. And if you want, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, well, have I been very busy working also on other trials. Also because of the specificity of the Gotovina, Cermak, Markac case, I only interacted with the two analysts, Dai Morris and Andrei Shakhmetov, who, as I explained, are the military analysts for this case. And I'm -- if you want I can readdress the interaction. They provide me with spreadsheets. I asked them whenever there was mention made of an archives mission, I provide them with a list of documents I would like to have. And it could be that I asked them some practical questions about availability of translations or similar issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you hadn't interviewed witnesses. Had those other members of the team interviewed witnesses of the Prosecution in this case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- I believe they did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know what interviews they took part in?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, over the years we have obviously spoken to each other and I heard that in the past, for example, Dai Morris participated in interview missions. I'm not sure about his role in those, whether he was actually interviewing or just assisting, and I have no clear recollection of whom he exactly interviewed or participated in the interview of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know what the content of those interviews revealed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The scope of your report, would you agree, is on the structure of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia in 1995 with periods prior as being relevant?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small addition, Your Honours, the answer is yes. But based on my review of the Croatian legislation, the special police is not identified as a component of the Croatian army as such, or Croatian armed forces, and therefore I wish to add that I also reviewed the structure, role, mission, command and control of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was going to my second question. I deliberately separated the topics. It also included the structure of the civilian parts of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I spoke about -- I speak about command and control over the armed forces which obviously points at the Supreme Command, i.e., the president. I also address the minister and Ministry of Defence. And in relation to police, I have provided minimal background information on the Ministry of Interior and the other police forces and have focussed my attention in the report on the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You also addressed the issue of the civilian authority in Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I addressed the role of General Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison between the 6th of August and around November. And if you want I can specify the end date, November 1995. And my conclusion in that context is that General Cermak was not only the garrison commander but exercised powers one would normally expect from purely civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The documents that you considered for the scope of your report on those three broad headings, and I was deliberately not specific as we are just dealing with general issues at this stage, was based upon documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct for -- for -- let's say for 95 per cent. As I also -- in particular these American military regulations, I looked for information on the Internet and had that material then introduced in evidence, and then, after my activity, it became available to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dealing with the scope, then, and the methodology, your methodology relies upon what you acquired as knowledge during your research. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that is not right. The methodology I applied and I explained also in -- relies on the knowledge I knew before joining the Office of the Prosecutor, which was in 2001, and also on the knowledge I acquired before starting this report, which was in January 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't have any pre-existing materials that form the bulk and substance of this report, did you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean that I didn't have a kind of personal set of -- of documents dealing with the issue, dealing with the issues covered in the report, then it is correct. But I just want to make a distinction between having physical documents and having prior knowledge or expertise of a certain topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the first time that you've addressed the issues within the scope of your report during your career. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Certain aspects of my report I also had to address or I also addressed while working as a military information officer in the UNPROFOR/UNPF headquarters, in particular during the months of August and September 1995. And some aspects I also addressed in a different form, not in an expert report but doing briefings, written assessments I prepared while working for the Belgian Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not talking here about the old JNA regulations or anything like that. The purpose of my question concerns those -- the scope of your report as it applied to the Republic of Croatia, which is why I summarized the areas as I did. Putting it in the round, would it be right to say that the laws and regulations that have been produced by you in your report, as well as the orders, decisions, other paper documents that are footnoted in your report, were put before you for the first time after you started your study in January 2007.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, the question is very broad in general. I remember -- just to give you an example, I remember that I was serving in the UNTAES, United Nations Transitional Administration in Eastern Slavonia, between July 1996 and May 1997, I was requested about the military information officers of the -- of our subordinate battalions as well as members of the military command whether I could compile a kind of guide on the political and military structure of Croatia. And then indeed I contacted members of political affairs office in the UNTAES headquarters as well as civil affairs in order to obtain, for example, copies of the constitution, documents in relation to military structure. I had access to Croatian military magazines, for example. There may have been some regulations but obviously not to the extent as I had now. And I used that information to draft a kind of a basic guide on political and military structures in Croatia, which was reviewed by the competent people in the political affairs department in the UNTAES headquarters before we -- before it was sent to the battalions that were part of the UNTAES peacekeeping force. That is just -- I'm sorry that I am so extensive, Your Honours, but it's just a example to show that I have worked on these issues prior to joining the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree those are very general documents and the documents as well as internal orders and commands, documentation that has been produced through units, battalions, brigades, institutions, were not materials that you had ever seen before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that I had not seen, for example, the specific attack order, Kozjak 1995 by the Split Military District, but I wish to draw your attention to the fact that these documents are established in accordance with certain templates, and I was familiar with these templates from my training in the Belgian military. Some of these documents, from the question of template, layout and concept, I also had seen and analysed during my activities on other cases. I knew, for example from my work in Belgium, what a war diary is why it is important, even though we give it another name. Now, I know, for example, from my work in the Vukovar trial that the war diary, there of the Guards Brigade, is an essential piece of evidence for that case. Well, that assisted me in assessing and understanding the important of the war diary and the operations diary of the Split Military District during Operation Storm, prior to and during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those are very general documents that are well known. Your expertise was not of a general nature but of a specific nature for the purpose of this report, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll put limb two of the question then. Essentially these documents were being produced to you for the structure of this report, and you were learning, on the job, about the inner workings of the Croatian armed forces and the civil and political structures.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the answers I have given to previous questions, in my view, show the opposite. And I will try to rephrase it as it is -- including my public CV. If at a certain moment in time I'm appointed to provide the daily -- the Balkan section of the daily intelligence briefing to the chief of Defence Staff in Belgium and the members of the Defence staff, well, I have been appointed because somebody considered me able of addressing not only -- of not only providing the briefing but also addressing the questions the chief of Defence Staff may have. And these questions well, cannot be answered if one had not a sound understanding of the political and military background to the conflict as well as the -- for example, the role and attitude of the international community to the conflict. So again it is not on January 2007 that I discovered -- in January 2007 that I discovered that there was a Croatian army, that there was a special police, that there were garrisons and they have an operational diary. When I read the -- and it's Exhibit P71, for the first time and I saw the entry, like, working meeting, I knew exactly what it was. In a sense that I had participated in such meetings not only in UNPROFOR but also when I was stationed in Germany and I understand -- I understood the importance of such a meeting, what is being said, what is not being said and why, and also the importance of -- of the comments made by the commander. And I'm just using that as an example but I can go into many more details, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's no issue that you can produce, collect and identify documents that are given to you, Mr. Theunens. That's not -- not the issue. The issue is whether you are an expert on the matters sufficiently to advise the Court, that you know enough about those subjects within the scope of the report or whether you were learning those detailed matters whilst on the job. You came with a certain level of knowledge, experience, no doubt about it, and have been to the basic courses within the Belgian military and the basic training, and you have been an analyst, you've been -- as you describe, but it's about the Croatian system, which the issue is here, as to whether your -- the methodology, putting documents before you, you were learning about the structure on the job.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will -- I'm afraid that I will be repetitive but I want to emphasise that it was not just about that somebody put documents in front of me. It is correct that I received spreadsheets but I also -- I did my own searches, and it's difficult to say but my guess would be that at least 30 per cent of the documents that are included in the report are documents that I found myself. I didn't check for each and every document whether it was included in a spreadsheet or not. That was not my concern. My concern was to determine whether the document was relevant. That relevancy was established by me only based on the methodology I applied. The methodology implies previous knowledge. Again, if I give briefings in UNPROFOR to the Force Commander, and in case of serious developments to the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, and I'm designated for that, it was not me, myself, who decided that. I assume that those who decided to -- I'm just stopping for the transcript. That those who decided to appoint me in order to give those briefings knew what they were doing. I'm not familiar with the criteria they applied, but I think it is relevant for the Court to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac, and he will now cross-examine you on this area. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From your CV and from what you've stated here we were able to see that in the course of your education you attended courses, various courses in Belgium and elsewhere. However, I did not find anywhere that you attended a course or that have you any specific knowledge on the issue of the special police force. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe there two components in the question. The first is whether I attended a particular course on the Croatian special police, and there the answer is no. The second component is whether I had knowledge of the special -- or have knowledge of the special police. Without entering, again, in what we discussed in closed session yesterday, I can state that I had knowledge of the doctrine, mandate, role, missions, deployment, and related issues of the Croatian special police prior to joining the ICTY in June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you attended several courses in physics and chemistry and that, nevertheless, you do not consider yourself to be an expert in these fields. Do you consider yourself to be an expert in the field of the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is is not up to me to determine whether I am an expert or not. I believe that I have, over the years, both outside the ICTY as well as during my stay here, acquired sufficient knowledge and understanding of the Croatian special police in order to address the issue, the issues that are covered in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when I asked you whether you considered yourself to be an expert, I was referring to Mr. Waespi's question earlier today at page 47, line 12, who asked [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... expertise to go into the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: ... [In English] ... obviously from my work at ICTY, I did not have that expertise. [Interpretation] Will you agree with me that the special police force is part of the Ministry of the Interior and a civilian structure as a category?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the special police is indeed part of the Ministry of Interior. It is organised along military lines. Military ranks are used, at least for the senior hierarchy, and based on my review and analysis of the documents, it is used as a special military force for particular operations. At least during and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I have some difficulties in finding your reference to page 47. Was that today or was that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's 19th of November. Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Page 47, line 11 till 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my understanding is correct, Mr. Theunens, though you do not feel to be an expert as far as civilian structures go and even though the special police force is part of civilian structure, nevertheless you consider yourself to be an expert enough to provide an expertise on the issue of the special police. Is that correct or is that contradictory? What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that you summarize what I'm trying to say and I don't see a contradiction in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Have you ever read, Mr. Theunens, any professional study on the issue of the special police, the purpose, structure, and use of the special police units in peacetime and in combat? If so, can you please list them.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the question addresses documents or studies which are not referred to my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to receive an answer on the knowledge you previously had on the issue of the special police before writing the report. Have you ever read an article, book, or a specific study on the purposes and uses of the special police? If so, can you please state which.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before joining the ICTY, while I was working for the Belgian Ministry of Defence, I reviewed information that covers the question asked by Mr. Mikulicic. In addition, I -- during the time-period I served in UNPROFOR as well as UNTAES, we had access to local -- I mean to Croatian press, including military magazines and also other magazines that addressed specifically -- I remember articles that specifically addressed the role of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say, Mr. Theunens, that you base your expertise on the newspapers articles you've read concerning the role of the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I would like to refer you to the first part of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you personally written a study on the role and purposes of the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the -- the earlier document I mentioned, the one I compiled while serving in the UNTAES mission, on the civilian and military structures in Croatia also addressed special police. While I was a member of the Belgian armed forces I also gave the -- I call it the intelligence or the background briefing to the newly appointed ECMM observers who were sent for deployment. And obviously during that briefing I didn't only cover political -- general political, historical, military aspects but also special police, even though it was in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Initially, you told us that in several cases before this Tribunal you appeared as an expert witness. Have you ever appeared as an expert witness before this Tribunal or any other Tribunal to testify on the role of the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This will or this would be the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break now, and after the break we'll then continue, Mr. Waespi, third portion, substance of the expert's -- expert's report. We'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I saw that Mr. Theunens brought some books and, I think, articles with him that might relate to these disciplinary Articles my colleague Mr. Misetic requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you brought, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know -- the problem with books is never not to give to someone but to get it back. That's the experience of all of us. Now what would you like to do, to copy the titles or just have a look at it or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I will hand them back before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's even under judicial supervision that the books are returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to give them to Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say -- I mean, if you'll allow me, the first book is very interesting in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now, the draw the attention of the one being more of specific interest than the other and ... Then, Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first topic I would like to address is command and control and military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the report could be brought up, which is now P1013, marked for identification. And I'm interested in the executive summary, page 22, English, and I think it is the second translation, page B in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now you discuss command and control and military discipline in paragraphs 3 to 5 and 18 of this executive summary, and there one can find references to the body of the report. Now I'd like to discuss these two issues together because they are related. In relation to military discipline, in paragraph 18 of your summary you offer the following opinions. And that's the second sentence, third line, and I quote: "In 1995, a legal system to enforce military discipline and military justice exists within the Croatian armed forces." And the last sentence in this paragraph 18, it's on the next page in the English. I quote: "A review of the correspondence between the Split MD Command and its subordinate units shows that the discipline system described here above is enforced by Major-General Ante Gotovina in his zone of responsibility prior to Operation Storm/Oluja." Now I'd like to explore the basis for these conclusions, but let me first ask you: Do you stand by these two conclusions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I stand by these two conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's first look at the four documents, you call them regulations, that outline the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the first document I would like to look at, and hopefully, Your Honours, you have the list of topics and exhibits I'm going to discuss in front of you. This is -- it's called tab 8. This is 65 ter 3049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the Chamber has nothing in front of it which is still -- still has the status of 65 ter documents. If it's not in any way either marked for identification or admitted into evidence, so if -- I've seen that list of ten and then 17, but I think they were neither marked or [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, that is a different topic. I had sent around, about a week ago, to Defence counsel and, indeed, Chamber's staff a list of topics and documents to be used by the OTP in live testimony of Reynaud Theunens. And I had anticipated that it would be given to Chambers. I apologise for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber received it. You can proceed. We will have it on our screen in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. It's a useful document because it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's useful because it refers to the footnotes and the page numbers of the expert report, in which each of the exhibits I'm going discuss live is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So this first exhibit -- can you very, very briefly without going into substance explain, Mr. Theunens, what this regulation is about.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the July 1993 defence law of the Republic of Croatia. A defence law establishes or defines the armed forces, command and control over the armed forces, command and control within the armed forces, as well as addresses aspects of the duties of military personnel and also the structure of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to Article 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is page 39 in e-court, English, and page 18 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what are the principles of command and control based on your review of the materials and your expertise in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Article 49 defines two principles for command and control in the Croatian armed forces; namely, unity of command, which means that there is only one commander at a time; and the second principle, the obligation to carry out decisions, commands and orders of a superior. And of course, the obligation to carry out decisions implies that people, I mean subordinates, are held accountable for their implementation of this order, which can be seen in the second paragraph of this Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President [sic]. If we could move to Article 39, which means a little bit backwards. Can you explain the significance of Article 39, if anything, as it relates to command and control.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this Article relates to command and control to -- to the extent that when members of the armed forces carry out combat operations, according to this Article they shall always and under all circumstances observe the rules of the international laws of war and the humane treatment of the wounded enemy and prisoners and the protection of the population, as well as other rules of this law -- laws. And it is connected to an article which I have discussed in the section under command and control which states that orders that result in crimes -- or may result in crimes shall not be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to exhibit this document. It's a fairly large document, I think about 100 pages, but we believe it is an important document which I'm sure the Defence might go into it as well. So rather than limiting myself to the few Articles, my suggestion would be to have it admitted as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The expectation expressed by Mr. Waespi a realistic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Theoretically, I mean, I have no problem putting the law into evidence, Your Honour. It's -- I'm not sure the relevance of most of it, but be that as it may, we have no objection to it coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that particular situation I could join my colleague from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So no objections. Of course, we always try to keep the exhibits of a size which makes it manageable and not to destroy too much of our woods. There is no objection. I invite the Prosecution to further consider with the Defence whether we really need 100 pages, if we are invited to pay attention only to three or four of them. Therefore, for example, to consider whether the title page and perhaps one or two pages to put matters in context or perhaps often legislation also has a table of contents to, for example, have the table of content and the specific articles. Would you please consider that, Mr. Waespi. For the time being, no objection. Could we hear from you within, let's say, still this week whether a reduced version. Otherwise, it slips out of our mind. Madam Registrar, we already admit into evidence this document, which will be given what number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be given Exhibit number P1116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1116 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let move to D32. These are the service regulations of the armed forces, and I'd like to have Article 4 displayed. My first question is: How does this document relate to the previous one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the service regulations in the HV, but also in other armed forces, are more detailed than the defence law. Of course they have to be coherent, I mean the different documents, but here you will find very detailed information in relation, for example, to relations between members of the armed forces, aspects of, organisation for example, of barracks, garrisons, specific duties of commanders, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Now what is the significance, if any, of Article 4 to command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 4, Your Honours, lists the duties of a commander. They can be grouped in a number of categories covering training and combat readiness, discipline, as well as logistics, and, yeah, preparation of the armed forces. When you look at the Article, the third bullet stipulates that commanders of units in institutions of the Croatian army are responsible for military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let's move to the third regulation, and that's a new document, 65 ter 5690, and I'd like to go to Article 241. Can you again let us know, first, how that relates to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the cover page mentions, Your Honours, this is an amendment to the service regulations which we've seen before, and this amendment is intended to cover the Guards Brigades. The Guards Brigades are defined in this amendment, as well as the duties of the members of Guards Brigades, the duties of commanders of Guards Brigades, in particular in the area of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now Article 241, what -- what's the significance?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Article 241 defines the Guards Brigades. As the Article states, Guards Brigades are the professional component of the Croatian armed forces. The Article also defines or establishes that Guards Brigades are equipped with the most sophisticated weapons and equipment and also that particular requirements are imposed on the personnel of Guards Brigades, not only the commanders but also soldiers and -- yeah, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to Article 245. Does that give a foundation what you called particular requirements for the members and commanders of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. These requirements are explained in the first -- or described in the first five lines of this Article 245. For example, on the third line we see that the profile of a Guards Brigade member is a combination of high intelligence, physical endurance, self-control, initiative, self reliance, and strong will. In the third paragraph of the Article, the duties of guardsmen, i.e., that is a general term for members of the Guards Brigade, are addressed. And for example the last two bullets or the last -- excuse me, the -- not the last but the one just before on page 5, states that members -- or that a guardsman should be an example to the other armed forces and, okay, has a duty to behave or to act with exemplary behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And briefly, and we heard a lot of testimony about that, which units, if any, of the Guards Brigade were part of Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation -- I assume your question is in relation to the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So two Guards Brigades operated under the command of General Gotovina during Operation Oluja. The first one is the 4th Guards Brigade, which was the establishment Guards Brigade of the Split Military District. The second one was the 7th Guards Brigade which, even previous to Operation Storm, was at times subordinated to the Split Military District Command, and during the conduct of Operation Storm was again subordinated to the Split Military District, even though organically it belonged to another Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P1117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1117 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last of these four regulations is an exhibit already, P1007, Code of Military Discipline. And here I'm interested in Article 26 specifically. And this is page nine, English, and page four in B/C/S. And the Article reads as follows: "Commanders authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings against offenders who are not members of his unit if such measures are required for the purposes of maintaining order and discipline. Commanders of units, institutions and garrisons, barracks, camps, medical institutions, ship, port, et cetera, shall issue disciplinary measures to offenders who are not members of their organic unit if such measures are required for maintaining order and discipline." What is the significance, if any, of this Article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wish to note that Article 26 still does not have a complete translation and I think we went through this with a witness, Botteri, who was here. There is a word missing in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must be quite frank with you, I don't remember that detail. If I know what the missing word is, and I take it, Mr. Waespi, you would accept that, then please help us out, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is in the English -- or in the original if you look -- if we can scroll over, please, Madam Registrar, to the right, so can I -- yes. The -- yes, to the right, please. Fourth line, the phrase begins "ako" and it is: [Interpretation] If they are required and necessary [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... appear in the English translation. All that appears in the English is "necessary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... now it rings a bell. "Are required" and then apparently from what Mr. Misetic tell us, and now it rings a bell that we dealt with the matter, that the English translation most likely would have to read "are required and necessary for maintaining order and discipline."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how the interpreters or how the translation service would strictly interpret that word, but my understanding is there is a sense of urgency in the word "nuzne." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how vital it is for your question, but could you answer the question that was just put to you, Mr. Theunens. If need be it will be repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I remember the question. I believe this is an essential Article, and I want to emphasize that it is not so much a duty that is imposed on the commander but also a privilege that is given to him, because it means that if he is operating with his organic forces in his zone of responsibility and a member of another unit commits a violation of discipline, be it serious or not serious, he has the right to act. The right to act is essential because if he has no possibility to act against the violation, and there is an Article in the Code of Discipline that shows the importance of or why military discipline exists, and if you allow me that is in Article 7, which is on English page number 3, which I believe will better explain my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would assist you then could it be on the screen. Article 7. You said that was page ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Article 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will soon appear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is sufficient if we see Article 7. Your Honours, the Article explains the three aims of disciplinary measures. First of all, what is described as reforming the offender, i.e., make it clear to him or her that they have committed an offence and that therefore measures are taken in order to prevent repetition by the same offender. Secondly, educating other members of the armed forces because, of, course soldiers live in close groups. Military units operate very closely together. There's something which is known as -- I mean, at a higher level esprit de corps, but there needs to be some kind of cohesion in the unit which is essential for a unit to function. And thirdly, upholding the interests and discipline of the armed forces. So if a commander sees that members of the military who are not part of his unit but still in his zone commit a violation of discipline, it is in his interest to have discipline restored as soon as possible or at least measures taken as soon as possible in order to restore discipline because otherwise there is a risk that the members of his own unit may engage in a similar activity. Because again -- and you notice that when you're operating in direct connection or a direct relation with soldiers, when you allow an individual soldier to come late, the next day the whole platoon will come late. When you allow a soldier, for example, to be unshaven or in an untidy uniform in the morning at the gathering, the next day most of them will do the same. So, again, the commander has an interest in enforcing discipline not only among his own troops but also among other troops that are acting or operating in his area in close presence of his own soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to Article 106, which is on page 25 in the English e-court version, and page 10 in B/C/S. This Article says that and I quote: "During wartime decisions on breaches, violations of military discipline shall be made immediately and not later than 24 hours from the moment of finding out." What's the significance, if any, of this to command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again it highlights the responsibility of the commander. And of course in war, troops are operating under pressure. Certainly goals have to be met. I mean, objectives have to be reached. There needs to be discipline in order to be able to implement these objectives or reach these goals that have been imposed by the superior commander. Article 106 has to be seen together with Article 105 because Article 105 talks about offences which are the -- as we can see in Article 6 of this Code of Discipline, offences of the more serious violations, whereas Article 106 talks about minor breaches, i.e., the less serious, yeah, breaches or violations of military discipline. And that is also explained in my report on page 169 in the English version, this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter. Looking at Article 106, I can't see it on the transcript, but my printed copy refers to minor breaches. I don't think Mr. Waespi read that out and I think it is important on this technical matter where we're not summarizing general documents. I have been guilty of that in the past for speed, but this of a technical nature to have the record right on that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, and I'm grateful for that to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you one last question on this Article 106, about the time-frame. What is the significance, if any, of the fact that these decisions have to be taken immediately and not later than 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most obvious reason for this is obligation, Your Honours, is that during wartime, well, events are happening 24/7. They are happening continuously. It's not like in peacetime where, during the day, from 8.00 to 5.00, troops are in the barracks or maybe conducting an exercise and then they go home. Here they're operating continuously, and because of this continuity there is a need to act urgently in case of violations of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. For the sake of the precision, I think the witness should be asked whether the wartime has been proclaimed in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking myself whether this is a matter to be raised in cross-examination or -- but perhaps, Mr. Waespi, it would be -- we would be better able to follow the testimony of this witness if we would know whether there's an issue there whether the formal proclamation of a time of war is relevant for this Article. So you're invited to explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean, this is connected with the implementation of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear from the witness or it may become clear to us on the base of the questions what the issue exactly is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether Article 106 applied during the time prior and during Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment I do not remember whether a state of war was formally declared in Croatia or was formally existing in Croatia at the time of Operation Storm. I remember that it existed at times in 1991. I remember that it had been lifted sometime I believe at the end of 1991, but I'm not -- I don't remember at this stage whether it had been reimposed in 1995. So in strict sense, if the state of war had not been declared, then one could argue that these two articles do not apply. Still military measures that would correspond with the declaration of a state of war, and I mean by that an increase in combat readiness as well as mobilisation of units, such measures were indeed taken during Operation Storm -- excuse me, prior to Operation Storm. They are discussed in the second part of the report, and from that I would conclude that even if formally the Articles may well not have applied, that the commander had all interests -- I mean the commanders at all levels had all interests in abiding by the provisions of these Articles during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let's move on now to the implementation of this doctrine. The next document is again an admitted document, P1020. This is a document dated 6 March. Can you briefly, without going into substance, characterize the document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is an example of the implementation of Article 26 of the 1992 Code of Military Discipline. We see that General Gotovina forwards a report of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, i.e., the military police battalion of the Split Military District, in relation to a traffic violation committed by a member of the 7th Guards Brigade. We see that Gotovina forwards that report to the commander of military post 3112 in Varazdin which corresponds with the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is there a relationship to Article 26 we just discussed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The 7 Guards Brigade is not an establishment or an organic unit of the Split Military District. It belongs to the Bjelovar Military District, which is located in northwestern Croatia. And because General Gotovina assesses or judges that this is not an urgent matter or not of urgency in order to maintain order and discipline in his zone of responsibility, he forwards the matter to the commander -- to the organic commander of the perpetrator but he asks him, i.e., he asks the commander of the 7 Guards Brigade to keep the commander of the Split Military District informed of the measures he has taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let move to the next document, a new one, 65 ter 5575. This is a report on a traffic offender, signed by commander Brigadier Ivan Korade, dated 25th April 1995, and it's addressed to the Split Military District Command, legal affairs department. What is the significance of this document, if any, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the reply of the commander of the 7 Guards Brigade to the request of General Gotovina expressed in the previous document, and Brigadier Korade informs General Gotovina of the disciplinary measure he, i.e., Korade, has taken following the traffic violation and the report filed by the 72nd Military Police Battalion for the traffic violation committed by a member of the 7 Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not still sure of the foundation for why this is being put in the context of Article 26. So ... I mean, with that caveat I ... if we could get some more foundation. I mean, Article 26, as far as I understand the witness's testimony thus far, is the commanders of the Split Military District could issue discipline against subordinated units. I don't see where that is taking place and if that's the proposition I would ask for more foundation on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, yes, if you are willing, of course, we could -- there's no clear objection against but it might assist the Chamber if would you follow the suggestion made by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Theunens, can you explain the relationship between this document and Article 26.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. When I read out the second line of Article 26, I'll start with the first line. It stated: Commanders of units and so on shall issue disciplinary measures to offenders who are not members of their organic unit if ... and so on, and then the conditions are explained, whether it is an urgent matter or not. Here we have an offender who is not a member of an organic unit of the Split Military District. The 7 Guards Brigade is not an organic unit of the Split Military District. It is temporarily subordinated to the Split Military District at the time of the -- of this violation, but it is not an organic establishment unit. From the organic point of view -- I'm sorry for the English. The 7 Guards Brigade belongs to the Bjelovar Military District which is located in northwestern Croatia along the border with Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection remains. The question is: Did General Gotovina issue a disciplinary measure to the subordinated unit? You know, my objection is to the foundation and I still haven't heard the answer -- it is clear that is being offered for that purpose, but where's the disciplinary measure by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, was it just meant as an example of reporting and to what extent does that follow within the scope of Article 26. That apparently is the issue. It has been explained by the witness now that at least the matter deals with someone who is not a member of an organic unit of the Split Military District. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just reminded to make a further objection. This isn't on the 65 ter exhibit list either. I don't have a problem with it if, in fact, it can be explained how referral to a different Military District falls under Article 26 as if General Gotovina is issuing discipline. But if it's not, then I don't see why it should be added to the 65 ter list or why admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'd like -- we have indicated in our list, as we agreed, that the documents that are in italics, you know, would be new and I would obviously make an oral application to add it to the 65 ter list. Second, it is our position that General Gotovina exercises jurisdiction, disciplinary jurisdiction over these members that are temporarily assigned to their units, and that is an example of that exercise. And I don't want to give evidence but that's what the witness explains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently it's a first step of reporting, which might lead to -- or is that misunderstood, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct. It is up to him what he does. But that is within his perogative to deal and his duty to deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that is how Mr. Ivan Korade looks at it, apparently -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...Mr. Korade looks at that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Enclosed please find a copy --let me just take time to read the whole of the document. If you would give me time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apparently the Split Military District Command is informed about a disciplinary measure which has been imposed upon a member of the 7th Guards Brigade. That's apparently what the document says. Now, Mr. Waespi, the issue raised by Mr. Misetic is whether this is a relevant document for the Prosecution's position, that the Split Military District Command, to whom this information was sent, was competent to exercise disciplinary powers over this non-organic unit that. Apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My position is this, Your Honours. And I believe we went through this once, although not with this specific document but with a prior witness who was actually personally involved in this, that what has happened here, and you can read it on its face, is that a report is submitted to the Split Military District by the military police. It is not ordered by General Gotovina, it is referred to a different section of the Croatian army and then is asked to report back as to what measure is taken. I don't see how that's interrelated to Article 26 of a commander issuing discipline against a subordinated unit, and so my objection is to the lack of foundation to support that assertion with this witness. If they can explain how this is a disciplinary measure as opposed to simply a referral to the proper authority to take discipline, then that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- usually we ask the witness to leave the courtroom if we discuss these kind of matters, but in the present circumstance it might be a very good thing that he hears it. You see that the relevance of this document is in dispute between Prosecution and Defence. Could you help us out, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, Mr. President. It would be helpful if we could see Article 26. I don't know whether that is technically feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, if we could have a look at it. But if you already start explaining, apparently you have Article 26 on your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. The second paragraph of Article 126 states that in situations where an officer under paragraph 1, i.e., the non-organic commander, has decided that it is not necessary that an offender who does not belong to his unit be immediately punished, the matter shall be forward to the offender's superior officer to deal with. So again, summarizing Article 26, Article 26 states that the commander can take disciplinary measures against members of non-organic units. This -- in case there is an urgency to take disciplinary measures or to have these disciplinary measures taken, he can do it himself. If he considers, i.e., the commander, that the matter is not urgent, he can refer it to the organic commander of the offender. So here, this is obviously not an urgent matter.
